BREAKING: President Trump's capital gains tax cut discussions include "indexing" capital gains for inflation BEFORE taxes are calculated.

This would mean that taxes would be applied on gains adjusted for inflation.

For example, if you purchased a stock for $100,000 and sold it 5 years later for $200,000.

Under the current system, you would owe capital gains taxes on the full $100,000 gain.

But, if cumulative inflation over those 5 years was 20%, your inflation-adjusted cost basis would rise to $120,000.

This means you would only owe capital gains taxes on the $80,000 REAL gain, rather than the $100,000 nominal gain.

Trump has also suggested exemptions for sales of homes worth $2 million or less from capital gains taxes.

We expect more details soon.

.@PalmerLuckey says every generation fights the new thing, and no generation fights to bring the old one back:

"People are saying, 'Oh my God, AI is gonna ruin everything.' How many people said the same thing about automated manufacturing?  The reality is that it actually made cars from a plaything for the rich into something that anybody can do."

"I feel like we're unfortunately in one of those swings where everyone is questioning whether technology will make our future better. I think it's especially unfortunate because we're on the precipice of so many things that have been scarce becoming unscarce."

A handful of stocks now dominate US market trading:

Nvidia, $NVDA, is the most actively traded stock in the US market, accounting for 3.0% of total market notional volume year-to-date.

This is followed by Micron, $MU, at 2.8%, Tesla, $TSLA, at 2.1%, and SanDisk, $SNDK, at 1.5%.

Together, the 10 most-traded stocks have accounted for an average of 16.4% of total market notional volume YTD.

Meanwhile, some of these names have worse liquidity than the average S&P 500 stock, with SanDisk posting an average bid-ask spread of 12.4 basis points, more than double the S&P 500's 5.9 basis point average.

Tesla, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Alphabet, $GOOGL, also have smaller average order sizes available at the best bid and offer than the typical S&P 500 stock, suggesting thinner liquidity despite their enormous trading volumes.

A few stocks a driving a massive amount of market volume.

"These agents are trained on existing code, and they have a reward structure. If code is meant to solve the bug, but it gets rewarded on that, it doesn't care if it's doing something else outside of that."

Investors are hedging less.

The 1-month put-to-call skew is down to 1.15 points, the lowest since April 2025.

This metric measures how much more investors are paying for downside protection against a stock market drop compared with bets on further gains.

Skew has fallen -0.13 points over the last 4 weeks, a similar decline to the one seen in April 2025 following the "Liberation Day" selloff and subsequent tariff pause relief rally.

Furthermore, the 3-month call skew is up to 0.9 points, the highest in at least 12 months.

This metric measures how much more investors are paying for far-out-of-the-money call options, which only pay off in a large market rally, compared to at-the-money calls.

Investor risk appetite is off the charts.

🇺🇸 Nearly 13% of credit card balances are now more than 90 days delinquent, close to levels seen around the Global Financial Crisis. However, once you dig into the data, the picture is much more nuanced as the US consumer is under pressure, especially at the lower end, but we are still far from a genuine credit crisis.

💳 The key point is precisely about credit cards as that 12.8% figure measures the stock of distressed debt, which includes old balances that banks have already charged off but that can remain on consumers’ credit reports for a long time. The NY Fed shows that changes in reporting practices explain a significant part of the rise seen over the past several quarters.

⚠️ To understand whether conditions are actually deteriorating right now, it makes more sense to look at the flow of new balances becoming seriously delinquent, and there, the picture is far less dramatic. The rate is around 7% and virtually unchanged from a year ago. An elevated rate, of course, but it suggests that the sharp deterioration seen between 2022 and 2024 has broadly plateaued. We are also still well below the roughly 11% reached during the financial crisis.

🚙 The area where I am more cautious is auto credit as balances continue to rise, originations are picking up, the average credit quality of new borrowers has weakened slightly, and delinquencies remain elevated, particularly among 18-29 year-olds, where serious delinquency rates are approaching 5%. The US consumer is not uniformly weak and the economy is increasingly two-speed. A homeowner who refinanced a mortgage at 3% in 2021, owns financial assets and benefited from rising house prices is in a completely different position from a young renter financing a car at 9% and carrying credit card debt at more than 20%.

➡️ My takeaway is fairly straightforward, the US consumer is weakened but not breaking. Some groups are clearly under significant pressure but credit deterioration no longer appears to be accelerating and there is still no evidence of a systemic accident. What I would watch from here is the combination of rising unemployment with renewed acceleration in credit card and auto delinquencies, and tighter bank lending standards.

➡ If all three start moving in the wrong direction at the same time, the story becomes much more concerning.

*Link: https://t.co/Fa1NRNDjzl

A homeowner who refinanced a mortgage at 3% in 2021, owns financial assets and benefited from rising house prices is in a completely different position from a young renter financing a car at 9% and carrying credit card debt at more than 20%.

➡️ My takeaway is fairly straightforward, the US consumer is weakened but not breaking. Some groups are clearly under significant pressure but credit deterioration no longer appears to be accelerating and there is still no evidence of a systemic accident. What I would watch from here is the combination of rising unemployment with renewed acceleration in credit card and auto delinquencies, and tighter bank lending standards.

➡ If all three start moving in the wrong direction at the same time, the story becomes much more concerning.

thread_tweets.text:
You're confusing consensus with relay.

Consensus rules never had a limit on opreturn, this defines the factual size of the wall.

Relay policy did have a limit, but this does not stop larger opreturns since they are consensus valid.

What happened was the POLICY limit was removed after the facts showed two things:
1) Devs continued putting non-monetary inside transactions. This was net negative, and OPRETURN was a more appropriate p[lace (because graffiti cannot be stopped).

2) Liberal relays had proliferated, and this meant the POLICY opreturn limit was totally ineffective. If Core had left it or removed it, the factual outcome was always going to be the same.

@give_cat_9sushi Probably because it's the literal worst place to ever post such data. An immutable public record that is heavily surveilled and tracked.

The reason nobody does it, is because it's a guaranteed trip to prison.

@Bitcoinfinity And who are you again?

It's pretty simple, there i no way to stop devs hiding data somewhere in the transaction data. Impossible.

Therefore, it's best put into an OP_RETURN which does NOT bloat the UTXO set. It's a graffiti wall in a world where graffiti cannot be stopped, no matter how many rules you make against it.

It really isn't that hard to understand tbh.

The wall was already that big, nodes like libre relay had already found ways to tell everyone about it. Usage of larger OPRETURNS came long before Core changed the default.

In effect, the asymmetry of relay policy, where only a few nodes need to be liberal to propagate transactions (hence filters are ineffective) meant the filter was ineffective.

They removed a redundant filter that graffiti artists were already well versed in bypassing.

You're confusing consensus with relay.

Consensus rules never had a limit on opreturn, this defines the factual size of the wall.

Relay policy did have a limit, but this does not stop larger opreturns since they are consensus valid.

What happened was the POLICY limit was removed after the facts showed two things:
1) Devs continued putting non-monetary inside transactions. This was net negative, and OPRETURN was a more appropriate p[lace (because graffiti cannot be stopped).

2) Liberal relays had proliferated, and this meant the POLICY opreturn limit was totally ineffective. If Core had left it or removed it, the factual outcome was always going to be the same.

tweets.text:
Your proposed fork didn't achieve rough consensus.

Instead of reflecting on why your proposal failed, you blame the referee, and the rules of the game, claiming a shady cabal has designed them to work against you.

You wanted to play chess by reverting the two pawn moves forward rule. The majority signalled that they did not want to play with those rules. The obvious result is nobody outside your little clique sat down to play your version.

The problem isn't with the existing rules of chess, nor those who currently enjoy playing by them.

The problem is that your proposal for changed rules was unappealing, and the attempt to force feed it to us didn't land...at all.

The new plan seems to be forking into some mutant form of checkers. Best of luck with that.
